title: Psalm 114: When Israel Came Out of Egypt
summary: In eight vivid verses the psalm retells the exodus and the entry into the promised land as a scene in which nature itself reacts to God. The sea flees, the Jordan turns back, and the mountains skip like rams. The poet asks them why, and then calls the whole earth to tremble before the God of Jacob, who turns rock into springs of water.
story: Psalm 114 is the second psalm of the Egyptian Hallel (Psalms 113 to 118) and the only one that tells the exodus directly. Psalm 113 praised the God who lifts the lowly; Psalm 114 shows him doing so for a whole nation of slaves. It compresses Israel's founding story, from leaving Egypt through the crossing of the sea, the trembling at Sinai, the water from the rock, and the crossing of the Jordan, into a single burst of poetry. For the returned exiles of Book V, who had lived through a second captivity and a second return, the first exodus was the pattern for everything God was doing again.
historical:
The psalm has no heading. Its compact, vivid language and its reference to Judah and Israel together have led some scholars to date it early, in the time of the united monarchy or soon after; others think it was composed later for festival use, drawing on older traditions. It was sung at Passover as part of the Hallel, and it fits that setting exactly. In the Greek Septuagint and in some Hebrew manuscripts, Psalms 114 and 115 are joined as a single psalm, which is one reason why psalm numbers differ between some Catholic and Orthodox Bibles and Protestant ones.

The events behind the psalm are told in Exodus and Joshua: the sea parting (Exodus 14), the mountain quaking when God came down on Sinai (Exodus 19:18), water from the rock at Horeb and at Meribah (Exodus 17:6; Numbers 20:11), and the Jordan stopping so the people could cross into Canaan (Joshua 3). The exodus is dated in two main ways, to the fifteenth century BC based on 1 Kings 6:1, or to the thirteenth century BC based on other evidence, and the psalm does not depend on settling that debate.
cultural:
An ancient reader would hear the sea and the river as more than water. In Canaanite myth, known from texts found at Ugarit on the Syrian coast, the storm god Baal fought a divine enemy called Prince Sea and Judge River. Psalm 114 pairs the sea and the Jordan in the same way, but there is no battle: the sea simply sees God and runs away. The waters that terrified the ancient world are pictured as frightened creatures.

The people of foreign tongue in verse 1 are the Egyptians, whose language Israelites did not understand; the word suggests speech that sounds like stammering. The images of verse 4, mountains skipping like rams and hills like lambs, come from shepherd life and carry a note of playful exaggeration, as though the rocky hills themselves have become a startled flock. Flint in verse 8 is the hardest stone of the desert, the least likely source of water.
literary: Psalm 114 is a small masterpiece of Hebrew poetry. It has four stanzas of two verses each. Verses 1 and 2 state the event; verses 3 and 4 describe nature's response; verses 5 and 6 repeat that response as mocking questions addressed to the sea, the Jordan, the mountains, and the hills; verses 7 and 8 give the answer. The poet withholds the name of God for as long as possible. In the Hebrew, verse 2 says Judah became “his” sanctuary without naming who he is, and only in verse 7 is the Lord, the God of Jacob, finally named. The effect is suspense: something has made the whole world recoil, and the reader must wait to be told who.

outline.t: Israel leaves Egypt and becomes God's dwelling
The sea, the Jordan, and the mountains react
Taunting questions: why did you flee?
Tremble before the God who makes rock into springs

doctrines.note: The exodus is the Old Testament's great act of salvation, a rescue from slavery by God's power alone. The psalm celebrates it not as a past event only but as a revelation of who God is.
Sea, river, and mountains obey and fear their maker. The natural world is not divine or autonomous; it responds to the presence of the God who made it.
Judah became God's sanctuary, the place where he dwells. The purpose of the exodus was not only freedom from Egypt but a people in whom God would live.

words.note: Qodesh, holiness or holy place, here “sanctuary.” The psalm does not say that God gave Judah a sanctuary but that Judah became his sanctuary. The people themselves are the dwelling of the holy God, an idea the New Testament develops when it calls the church God's temple.

Memshalah, dominion or realm. Israel became the territory over which God rules as king. Taken with sanctuary in the same verse, it shows that the exodus created a people who were both God's temple and God's kingdom.
Chul, to writhe or tremble, sometimes used of labor pains. The earth is told to tremble at the presence of the Lord. The word conveys a whole-body shaking in the face of overwhelming power.

Tsur, rock. The rock that gives water recalls the wilderness miracles, and elsewhere in the Psalms God himself is called the Rock of his people. The psalm ends not with terror but with provision: the God who shakes mountains opens springs for the thirsty.

christ: The New Testament uses the exodus as a primary pattern for understanding Jesus. At the transfiguration, Luke says Moses and Elijah spoke with Jesus about his departure (Luke 9:31), using the Greek word exodos, the death and resurrection by which he would lead his people out of a greater slavery. Paul, reflecting on the wilderness, says the Israelites drank from a spiritual rock that followed them, and the rock was Christ (1 Corinthians 10:4). Jesus himself offered living water to the thirsty (John 7:37-38). These are New Testament readings of the exodus pattern rather than predictions within Psalm 114, but they show the church hearing in this song the shape of its own rescue.
questions: The psalm asks the sea why it fled. What in your life seemed immovable until God's presence changed it?
Judah became God's sanctuary. What does it mean for a community of believers today to be the place where God lives?
The God who makes mountains skip also turns flint into a spring. Where do you need to trust him for provision in a hard and dry place?
